sources.fullCitation: “United States-Mexico border crossing, Calexico, [1927?].” Los Angeles Times Photographic Collection, Library Special Collections, Charles E. Young Research Library, University of California, Los Angeles. Black-and-white nitrate negative, local identifier uclamss_1429_0385, ark:/21198/zz002d9ndg. A bird's-eye view of the crossing showing two security booths, cars and pedestrians, an arcaded building on the Mexican side and a sign arching over the road reading “Mexico”, with further signs for Mexicali, Southern Club Cafe, Cafe Gabrinus and Climax Cafe. The negative sleeve is annotated “Mexican American Line, Calexico, Mexicali” and “California, Calexico-Mexicali”. UCLA suggests a possible connection to two Los Angeles Times reports from Calexico, “No Permit Needed at Mexican Border” of 6 July 1927 and “New Regulations in Force at Border” of 14 July 1927, but does not confirm publication. UCLA states the item as copyrighted, names itself as rights holder, and licenses it under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International. Accessed 3 August 2026.

media.title: United States–Mexico border crossing at Calexico, c. 1927
media.altText: Bird's-eye photograph of the United States–Mexico border crossing at Calexico, with two security booths, cars and pedestrians passing under a sign reading Mexico.
media.publicCaption: The Calexico–Mexicali crossing photographed for the Los Angeles Times about 1927. Kaper entered the United States here on 1 November 1935, eight years after this view was taken, so the picture shows the place rather than the day.
media.publicCreditLine: Los Angeles Times Photographic Collection, UCLA Library Special Collections, Charles E. Young Research Library; uclamss_1429_0385, ark:/21198/zz002d9ndg. Licensed CC BY 4.0.

Had the photograph been published in 1927 it would in any case be public domain in the United States, the ninety-five-year term having expired in 2022, but UCLA links it to the July 1927 reports only as a possibility and does not confirm publication, so the licence rather than expiry is the basis relied on here.
